title: Inside the Not-So-Dumb Head of the Dodo Bird
gist: Digital endocasts of three museum dodo skulls, published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, show the dodo’s forebrain was proportionately as large as in 36 living pigeons and doves, while its optic lobes were more than 3.5 times smaller — pointing to a low-light, smell- and touch-guided bird rather than a stupid one. The species’ reputation traces to first-contact impressions and Linnaeus’ 1766 name Didus ineptus, not to evidence.

themes.theme: A reputation built on first contact, not evidence

insights.claim: The dodo’s reputation for stupidity originates with European sailors on Mauritius who read its ground-dwelling gait and lack of fear as foolishness, and was then formalized by Linnaeus, who classified it as Didus ineptus in 1766.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Case study in how an early observational label gets locked into taxonomy and survives centuries without testing.
insights.quote: they could only think to call it one thing: a “dodo.”
insights.locator: Dodo birds got a bad rap from the very start

insights.claim: The dodo was turkey-sized, completely flightless despite having wings, and went extinct in 1662, and is now classified as Raphus cucullatus.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Basic species facts needed to weigh the brain-size comparisons against body size.
insights.locator: Granted, it was the size of a turkey

insights.claim: Researchers led by the University of Lethbridge scanned three dodo skulls held in natural history museum collections in Denmark and the United Kingdom, two of which are the only complete dodo skulls found to date.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: The entire evidence base for dodo neuroanatomy is two complete skulls — conclusions are precise but thinly sampled.
insights.locator: Led by researchers at the University of Lethbridge

insights.claim: Because a brain leaves an imprint on the inner surface of the skull, digitally reconstructing that cavity and comparing it with living birds recovers sensory and behavioral inference from an animal whose soft tissue vanished centuries ago.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Reusable method: extinct-species behavior can be reconstructed from cavity geometry plus a living comparative set.
insights.quote: “Although the dodo’s brain disappeared centuries ago, it left an imprint on the inside of the skull,”
insights.locator: Although the dodo’s brain disappeared centuries ago

insights.claim: Compared against brain imprints from 36 living Columbiformes, the dodo’s forebrain — the region handling memory and cognition — was proportionately similar in size, placing its cognitive hardware in the same class as pigeons and doves.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: The headline reversal: relative forebrain size, the standard proxy, gives no support for the “inept” label.
insights.locator: By comparing the dodo’s brain imprints

insights.claim: Pigeons show remarkable cognitive abilities such as long-term image recognition, so equivalence with pigeons is a meaningful floor rather than a weak baseline.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Sets the reference point that makes the dodo comparison informative.

insights.claim: The dodo’s tameness toward 16th-century sailors is better explained by a predator-free island history than by any deficit in intelligence.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Island naiveté, not stupidity, as the mechanism — the same framing applies to other insular species judged “dumb.”
insights.locator: may have stemmed more from their predator-free history

themes.theme: Sensory profile tuned for low light

insights.claim: The dodo’s optic lobes were more than 3.5 times smaller than a pigeon’s, a signature of vision adapted to low light such as dawn, dusk, and night rather than of poor eyesight overall.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Sharpest quantitative result in the piece and the basis for the crepuscular/nocturnal reinterpretation.
insights.locator: One distinction of dodo brains was their smaller optic lobes

insights.claim: Dodo skulls were high-domed in a way reminiscent of certain owls, converging on a form associated with low-light foraging.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Independent morphological line pointing to the same low-light lifestyle conclusion.
insights.locator: Furthermore, the high-domed skulls of dodos

insights.claim: Olfactory bulb imprints indicate a keen sense of smell that, combined with a pronounced upper beak used to probe the surroundings, would have let dodos forage without relying on bright-light vision.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Reframes the dodo as a sensory specialist — a trait profile, not a defect.
